title: IELTS Academic Writing Practice Test 3
instructions: You have 60 minutes for both tasks. Spend approximately 20 minutes on Task 1 and 40 minutes on Task 2.

questions.prompt: The pie charts show the proportion of household waste recycled in a particular city in 2005 and 2020. Summarise the main features and make comparisons where relevant.
questions.modelAnswer:
The two pie charts illustrate the changes in the proportion of different types of household waste recycled in a specific city between 2005 and 2020.

Overall, there was a noticeable increase in the recycling rates of plastics and glass over the fifteen-year period, while the proportion of cans and 'other' waste recycled decreased. Paper remained the most recycled material in both years, despite a slight decline.

In 2005, paper constituted the largest share of recycled waste at 30%, followed by 'other' waste at 25% and cans at 20%. Glass and plastics had lower recycling rates, at 15% and 10% respectively. By 2020, plastics saw the most significant rise, more than doubling from 10% to 25%, making it the second most recycled material. Glass recycling also increased from 15% to 20%.

Conversely, the proportion of cans recycled fell by 5%, from 20% in 2005 to 15% in 2020. Similarly, 'other' waste experienced a substantial drop from 25% to 12%. Paper recycling saw a minor decrease, moving from 30% to 28%, but still represented the highest category of recycled materials in the city.

questions.prompt: Some people believe that individuals should be responsible for reducing the amount of waste they produce; others think governments should enforce stricter recycling regulations. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The escalating problem of waste generation has prompted debate regarding the most effective approach to mitigation. While some advocate for individual accountability in minimising refuse, others contend that governmental intervention through stringent recycling laws is paramount. This essay will discuss both perspectives before arguing that a collaborative effort, underpinned by individual responsibility and government regulation, offers the most comprehensive solution.

Proponents of individual action assert that personal choices directly impact waste volumes. By consciously reducing consumption, reusing items, and responsibly sorting recyclables, individuals can significantly lessen their environmental footprint. For instance, opting for reusable coffee cups instead of single-use plastics or repairing broken appliances rather than discarding them are tangible steps that, when collectively adopted, contribute to a substantial decrease in landfill waste. This approach fosters a sense of personal ownership and promotes sustainable habits from the ground up.

Conversely, those who favour governmental enforcement argue that systemic change requires legislative backing. Without mandatory regulations, individual efforts may remain sporadic and insufficient to tackle the sheer scale of the waste crisis. Strict recycling laws, coupled with robust infrastructure for collection and processing, can ensure widespread compliance and create a uniform standard for waste management. A pertinent example is the deposit-return schemes implemented in various European countries, which have dramatically increased recycling rates for beverage containers by incentivising participation through a refundable fee.

In conclusion, while individual efforts are undeniably valuable, they are most effective when supported by a robust framework of governmental regulations. A holistic strategy that empowers individuals to make responsible choices while simultaneously enforcing stricter recycling mandates at a societal level will ultimately prove most successful in addressing the global waste challenge.
